works.idea: It began as a riff on a sampler and a drum pattern she sang out loud.

making.label: A room in the country
making.body: In 1983 Kate Bush moved to rural Sevenoaks and set up a writing room with a piano, a Fairlight CMI and an eight-track recorder. This was the first song she wrote for Hounds of Love, in a single evening.

making.label: Riff first, then a sung drum part
making.body: The song began with the Fairlight riff. She sang a drum pattern to Del Palmer, who programmed it into a LinnDrum. She said the first verse’s lyrics “came straight away”.

making.label: The demo became the record
making.body: She recorded a demo on eight-track. In early 1984 it was transferred to 24-track at her East Wickham Farm studio, where the riff was refined and parts, including the vocals, were recorded again with Palmer and engineers Paul Hardiman and Haydn Bendall.

making.label: A cello that used to be a harp
making.body: The main riff is a sampled cello on the Fairlight. It replaced a harp sound she found too noisy.

making.label: A frozen chord
making.body: The drone under the song was made by “freezing” a chord in a Quantec digital reverb.

making.label: People on top of the machine
making.body: Stuart Elliott overdubbed a snare to strengthen the LinnDrum’s and added fills at the end. Palmer played a “pulsing” bassline. Alan Murphy added guitar for the ending and Paddy Bush played balalaika.

making.label: The title
making.body: She called it “A Deal with God”. EMI thought that could cost it radio play. She agreed to change it, to “give the album a chance”.

making.label: The notes
making.body: It’s in C minor. The vocal melody leans on the minor seventh, which creates tension. On the word “could” she sings a major seventh over an A-flat major chord.

glossary.body: An early sampler. It records a sound and lets you play it back as notes on a keyboard.
A 1980s drum machine that plays recordings of real drums in a pattern you program.
One sustained sound held under everything else.
A part recorded later on top of what’s already there.

map.note: Placed by ear. The chords and the instruments are documented; where each one enters is our reading.

moments.label: From the first second
moments.body: The sound that never stops is one chord, frozen in a reverb.

moments.label: On the word “could”
moments.body: A major seventh over A-flat major. It’s the brightest, most hopeful note in the melody.

moments.label: The ending
moments.body: Real drum fills and a guitar arrive only here. Until now the rhythm has been a machine.

why: The drum pattern never plays a fill, so nothing ever lets the tension go. The song keeps running, like its title.

The melody leans on a note that wants to resolve and doesn’t. It matches a lyric about wanting something you can’t have. When humans finally play at the end, it feels like the release the machine refused to give.

tryIt.title: Sing the drums first
tryIt.body: Before touching a drum machine, sing or beatbox the pattern into your phone. Program what you sang, not what the grid suggests.

tryIt.title: Freeze a chord
tryIt.body: Play one chord into a reverb with a freeze or infinite setting and keep it under the whole song as a drone.

tryIt.title: Change the sound, not the notes
tryIt.body: If a part feels wrong, try the same notes on a different instrument before rewriting it. A harp became a cello here.

tryIt.title: Save the humans
tryIt.body: Keep the rhythm programmed for most of the song. Bring in one played instrument only for the ending.

works.idea: Three chords that never change, and a band that makes them sound like three different songs.

making.label: Written in ten minutes
making.body: Early 1976, at the Record Plant in Sausalito. Stevie Nicks found “a black-and-red room, with a sunken pit” and a piano she believed belonged to Sly Stone, sat at a Fender Rhodes and wrote the song “in about 10 minutes”.

making.label: A song the band found boring
making.body: Christine McVie heard the rough version and called it “just three chords and one note in the left hand”.

making.label: Same chords, three rooms
making.body: Lindsey Buckingham kept the chords and built three sections out of them, each made to sound different. That won McVie over.

making.label: A loop before loops were normal
making.body: Producer Ken Caillat cut eight bars of Mick Fleetwood’s drumming into a loop, for what he called a “deep hypnotic effect”.

making.label: The first vocal stayed
making.body: Nicks recorded ten lead takes. The one on the record is the guide vocal, with a few lines punched in.

making.label: Width from very little
making.body: The electric guitars were sent through four signals and spread across the stereo field. Buckingham worked out the chorus harmonies as triads on a piano; they were sung in three parts, then doubled.

glossary.body: A quick take sung so the band can follow the song while recording. It’s usually replaced later.
Re-recording just one line and dropping it into an existing take.
A short recording repeated end to end, so the feel never changes.

map.note: Placed by ear. The chords and the instruments are documented; where each one enters is our reading.

moments.body: Tom accents enter. The loop has been running untouched until here.

moments.label: Pre-chorus
moments.body: A vibraphone played through a delay, low in the mix.

moments.label: Chorus
moments.body: The only place all three voices sing. Try following the lowest one.

why: Most songs change chords to tell you a new section has started. Dreams can’t, so it changes the room instead: a new instrument, a wider guitar, more voices. Your ear reads that as movement.
The loop does the opposite job. It never reacts to anything, which is why the song feels calm even when the words aren’t.

tryIt.title: Three sections, same chords
tryIt.body: Take a two or three chord loop. Write a verse, a lift and a chorus over it without changing harmony. Only add, remove or widen parts.

tryIt.title: Loop your best eight bars
tryIt.body: Find the eight bars where the drummer sits best and repeat them for the whole song. Add accents on top by hand, like the toms at 0:48.

tryIt.title: Keep the guide
tryIt.body: Record the scratch vocal properly. Before replacing it, check whether the feel is already there and only fix the lines that need it.

versions.label: The Corrs, 1998
versions.body: Recorded close to the original for the tribute album Legacy, then turned into a dance track with violin and tin whistle by Oliver Leiber and remixed by Todd Terry. No. 6 in the UK.

versions.label: Deep Dish with Stevie Nicks, 2006
versions.body: An electronica remake with new vocals from Nicks herself. A top-20 UK hit.

versions.label: Jolyon Petch, 2021
versions.body: A club version that reached No. 1 on Australia’s ARIA Club Tracks chart.

versions.label: What to hear
versions.body: All three add a beat the original never had. The three chords survive every time.

making.label: Two people
making.body: Billie Eilish wrote it with her brother Finneas O’Connell in 2018. He produced it and she added production. Rob Kinelski mixed it and John Greenham mastered it.

making.label: Four sounds
making.body: The production is built from synth bass, a kick drum, amplified finger snaps and 808 bass. That’s nearly the whole record.

making.label: The riff is the chorus
making.body: Where a sung chorus would go there’s a synth riff, which critics called “goofy carnival” and “cartoony”. The words around it are half-spoken, ending on “duh”.

making.label: A crossing signal from Sydney
making.body: One sound is an Australian pedestrian signal. Eilish recorded it on her phone in February 2017.

making.label: Two tempos
making.body: The song has two halves. The first runs at 135 BPM, the second at 120.

making.label: Where it came from
making.body: Eilish named “Never” by JID and “Stuck in the Mud” by Isaiah Rashad as influences on the writing.

making.label: The chords
making.body: Reported as G minor, moving Gm–Cm–D7. The published source for this is weak, so check it against your own ears.

glossary.body: A deep, long bass note, named after the Roland TR-808 drum machine it first came from.
Beats per minute. 120 is a brisk walk; 135 is a jog.
The part you remember. Usually sung, but it doesn’t have to be.

map.note: Placed by ear. The chords and the instruments are documented; where each one enters is our reading.

moments.label: The riff
moments.body: Wait for the chorus and notice that nobody sings one. The synth line takes its place.

moments.label: The slow end
moments.body: The tempo drops from 135 to 120 BPM and the song becomes something heavier.

moments.label: The voice
moments.body: It sits right at the front and stays quiet. Turn it up and you’ll hear breaths and mouth sounds left in.

why: With only four sounds, each one is huge. There’s nothing for the bass to compete with, so it can be the melody, the rhythm and the weight at once.
Keeping the voice quiet and close makes the listener lean in. Loudness would have filled the space the arrangement worked to leave empty.

tryIt.title: Four sounds only
tryIt.body: Finish a section using four sounds and nothing else. When it feels thin, change a part instead of adding one.

tryIt.title: Let a riff be the chorus
tryIt.body: Mute your chorus vocal and write an instrumental line that does its job. See which one people hum afterwards.

tryIt.title: Change tempo once, late
tryIt.body: Write a final section 10 to 15 BPM slower than the rest. Keep one element from before so it still sounds like the same song.

tryIt.title: Record the street
tryIt.body: Capture one sound on your phone this week and put it in a track where a drum or an effect would normally go.

guide.label: Verse
guide.body: Listen to the bass line. It carries the song as much as the voice does.

guide.label: Chorus
guide.body: Notice the clipped, rhythmic phrasing that critics heard as a Michael Jackson influence.

observations.label: Reception
observations.body: Billboard called it “Michael Jackson-esque”; Vulture described a move to “neo-MJ”.

observations.label: Rhythm

dimensions.label: Arrangement

guide.label: The first second
guide.body: Three low piano notes. Blender wrote that the motif makes its presence known within the first second.

guide.label: Chorus
guide.body: Listen for how the opening motif returns under the chorus and ties the song together.

observations.label: Motif
observations.body: Opens with a three-note motif in the piano’s bass range, compared by critics to “We Will Rock You”, “Start Me Up” and the Jaws theme.

observations.label: Production

dimensions.label: Voice

dimensions.label: Pulse

dimensions.label: Arrangement
dimensions.body: Piano motif, guitar stabs and a big chorus.

dimensions.label: Made by

guide.label: Verse
guide.body: Listen to the guitar chords pulsing on every beat. They give the song its rush.

guide.label: Chorus

observations.label: Arrangement
observations.body: Guitar-driven pop with a constant eighth-note pulse rather than a dance beat.

dimensions.label: Voice

dimensions.label: Pulse

facts.label: Chart

events.title: Released as the lead single from Warrior
Withdrawn from various US radio stations
events.body: The day after the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, stations judged the title and chorus inappropriate for airplay.

guide.label: Throughout
guide.body: Listen for how rarely the track pauses. Short transitions keep it moving from section to section.

guide.label: Chorus
guide.body: Notice how the hook repeats in layers, so the song feels like one long chorus.

observations.label: Structure
observations.body: Hooks return in layers instead of resting on one isolated chorus, which keeps the energy constant.

observations.label: Instruments
observations.body: A full list of instruments and programmed parts has not been sourced yet.

dimensions.label: Voice
dimensions.body: Half-sung, half-chanted party delivery.

dimensions.label: Pulse
dimensions.body: A steady four-on-the-floor dance beat.

dimensions.label: Arrangement
dimensions.body: Dense, with layered hooks and few breaks.

dimensions.label: Made by
dimensions.body: Written by Kesha, Dr. Luke, Benny Blanco, Nate Ruess and Cirkut; produced by Dr. Luke, Benny Blanco and Cirkut.
